newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kongers prefer Hollywood.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kongers prefer Hollywood.

text.p: Hong Kong's moviegoers prefer Hollywood to handover.

An epic movie meant to stir their nationalist and anti-colonialist pride as they return to Chinese rule has flopped at the box office despite the earnest support of President Jiang Zemin and other leaders in Beijing.

"The Opium War" -- at US$15 million the costliest Chinese movie ever produced -- was made to remind Chinese how their country was humiliated in the war over opium trading which led to Britain seizing Hong Kong in 1841.
But Hong Kongers are walking past the marquee to see Bruce Willis in "The Fifth Element", the most popular show in town as the British furl their flags to go home.
"The Opium War" is ninth in the ratings, taking only HK$3.7 million in 13 days, a quarter of the amount spent on its Hollywood rival.
Asia's brightest-lit city will plunge briefly into darkness on Tuesday night when millions of multi-coloured lights along the waterfront make way for a blitz of fireworks and lasers.

"One hundred and thirty buildings and hotels on both sides of the harbour will synchronise the switching off, in order to improve the effect of the display," said a spokeswoman for the ceremony organisers, the Better Hong Kong Foundation.
The massive neon signs on glass and marble tower blocks beside Hong Kong harbour are a world tourist sight.
They have been enhanced recently by huge neon pictures with 1997 handover themes, orchids and dolphins.

The first gift that the Hong Kong people hand to their restored motherland after next week's merger will be a hospital train on a mercy mission providing free medical care to remote and poor corners of China.
The $19-million Lifeline Express, funded by Hong Kong donors, will set off on July 1, the day Hong Kong returns to Chinese rule.
"We chose to start out on July 1 as this makes the train a symbolic handover gift to China," said Angela Ng, executive director of the Lifeline Express.
With basic equipment and a 16-member medical team aboard, the train hopes to treat up to 3,000 people a year for cataracts and polio in poverty-stricken regions.
More than 10 million people in mainland China suffer from the afflictions.
The 4,000 official guests at the handover ceremony will each receive a designer wristwatch and a 220-page book of 320 views of Hong Kong as souvenirs.
Hong Kong is the world's second largest exporter of watches after Switzerland and the world's largest exporter of clocks.
A hail of "taxi!" won't help tens of thousands of revellers on the streets for the handover. Taxi drivers are taking the night off too.
